headline: No climate deal. The last time that happened was 2009.
summary: UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ran two days past their deadline and ended Sunday with no main agreement, the first collapse since Copenhagen in 2009. Monday's draft named fossil fuels six times. Sunday's named them zero times, and the EU, Panama and the Marshall Islands refused it. Smaller deals passed. Next try: Ethiopia, 2027.

cover_question.q: Is the Earth going to be OK?

cover_answer: It is getting warmer. The grown-ups are still working on it.
table_question: Should one person be able to block what everyone else agreed to?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Grown-ups from almost every country spent two weeks in one big room in Turkey, making a plan to keep the Earth from getting too hot. They stayed two extra days, like staying after the bell to finish a group project, and still went home without one. The Earth is getting warmer, and the grown-ups are on it. They meet again next year.
5-7.why: A group project that ran past the bell is a scene a six-year-old has sat in. The ending says the adults have not quit.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them and reads your face before your words, so the script keeps the picture small: a room, a bell, a project not finished. Nothing in it is a flood or a fire. Expect 'is the Earth going to be OK?' Say it is getting warmer and the grown-ups are still working on it, and say it calmly.

8-12.script: Burning coal, oil and gas heats the planet, so the EU and island nations wanted the deal to say so. Monday's draft said 'fossil fuels' six times. After Russia and Saudi Arabia pushed back, Sunday's said it zero times. A COP deal works like a jury: everyone has to agree, so the EU's no sank it.
8-12.why: Six to none is a chain they can count. A jury rule is how a few beat many.
8-12.why_long: At twelve a child is working out whether rules apply the same to everyone, and the numbers do the work: six mentions on Monday, none by Sunday, then a jury rule where one no beats a hundred yeses. Expect 'why don't they change the rule?' That needs the same unanimous yes, and the UN's climate chief says he is asking how to reform it.

13-17.script: Is a weak deal better than no deal? Palau said yes and would have signed. The EU, Panama and the Marshall Islands said no, and the longest climate talks in UN history ended with nothing. Second: a few oil states blocked a text most countries accepted. Keep a rule that needs everyone?
13-17.why: Palau and the Marshall Islands read the same text and split. A real disagreement beats a lecture.
13-17.why_long: A thirteen-year-old can hold two true things at once: the text was weak, and no text may be worse. Palau and the Marshall Islands read the same draft and split. Nobody has to invent a side. Expect 'so what was the point?' Bowen says the move off fossil fuels is happening anyway. Ask whether writing it down matters.

5-7.q: Is the Earth going to be OK?
5-7.a: It is getting warmer. The grown-ups are on it, and they try again next year.

8-12.q: Why did they need everyone to agree?
8-12.a: That's the rule here. Any country can say no, and the EU did.
Not nothing. Smaller deals passed, one for workers as energy changes.

13-17.q: Why would Palau sign a weak deal?
13-17.a: Its minister said it had clean electricity, ocean and finance in it.

13-17.q: Can anything stop oil states blocking it?
13-17.a: Not under this rule. The UN climate chief is seeking advice on reform.
